speechtext: 31. That the deductions from tax allowed to a corporation whose principal business is the production, refining or marketing of petroleum or petroleum products in respect of drilling and exploration costs be extended to oil wells spudded in during the year 1947 and the deepening of oil wells which is commenced in 1947 but that in respect of such wells the deductions be reduced from 261 per cent and 40 per cent of the cost to 20 per cent and 30 per cent respectively.
The last time this matter was under discussion the minister intimated that he would make a statement in connection with the oil industry.

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Acting Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I thought I had made my usual brief preliminary statement, and I was under the impression that the hon. member was going to make a few observations on these sections. However, I am prepared to repeat what I stated. These five resolutions, 31, 32, 33, 34 and 35, in effect continue the tax credits granted petroleum, natural gas and mining industries in respect of exploration expenditures for another year with proper adjustment for reduction of the flat rate tax on corporation income from 40 to 30 per cent. Also, under 31, the existing tax credit granted for expenditures incurred in any new oil well is extended to include expenditures incurred in deepening an existing well.

Just before we adjourned the other night I had drawn to the minister's attention some five suggestions which I had made earlier in the speech on the budget in regard to changes in the tax structure which would aid the oil industry, and I understood that the minister would make some comment thereon.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I apologize to my hon. friend. He is quite right; I had intended to give some consideration to the five suggestions he made. I understood the first to relate to the deepening of existing wells. That is being taken care of under the ordinary tax concession and not under the special 50
per cent arrangement. He asked in the second place that the tax concessions be extended to the drilling of shallow wells. That cannot be done. Third he asked that the 33J per cent be increased to 50 per cent, and there again we felt the request could not be granted. Fourth he asked that tax credits be made permanent. Here once more it is felt that we cannot accede. It must be made on the annual basis. The fifth suggestion related to the removal of the subsidy on imported oil. As my hon. friend will appreciate, that is not a tax matter. I shall be glad to discuss it when we reach the estimates of the wartime prices and trade board, where these subsidy items are provided for.

In connection with the request for extension of the fifty per cent tax drawback to completing wells, will the minister say whether the resolution means that the drawback will now apply to abandoned exploratory wells on which redrilling is started?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am advised that the
twenty per cent tax credit does, but not the fifty per cent.

Can the minister give any reason why this fifty per cent tax drawback will not apply to abandoned exploratory wells which people may now be willing to drill down to the oil-bearing strata? At the present time a considerable number of wells have been drilled in the foothills to considerable depths, but owing to the company's running out of money, or for other reasons, the wells were abandoned before they actually struck the oil-bearing lime. If this fifty per cent drawback were made available for these wells a considerable number of them would be completed.

Before the minister answers may I ask what is in one sense a supplementary question and in another a broader question? In dealing with this question is it the policy of the government to consider it from the point of view of maximum development of the industry? Is that the government's aim? If it is, I would hesitate to argue that any exemption be made permanent; nevertheless in making it merely annual it would seem to me to work against what one would expect to be the full encouragement of the industry. I am not as familiar with this matter as the hon. member for Calgary East, but I should be enlightened if the minister would tell us in much broader terms what is the principle on which the government is acting.
Income War Tax
speakername: Mr.   M A CD ON N ELL@Muskoka-Ontario

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
As my hon. friend is probably aware, this has been discussed at considerable length to my knowledge in at least three sessions of parliament. I have done a good deal of discussing of it myself. It is incentive legislation. It was introduced first during the war in order to encourage the production of oil in Canada. I must say that the concessions are appreciable, particularly the fifty per cent one which we are now discussing. It was felt that it should be granted on a year to year basis. In other words, a year in advance a prospective oil driller knows that if during the year he drills a certain type of well, conducts a certain type of exploration operations, he will be allowed a certain tax concession.
Answering my hon. friend's question as to what good reason there is for not making this apply to a well which has been abandoned and then started up again, may I say that subsection 10 of section 8, under which this concession is provided, sets out the conditions. In the first place the enterprise must be one which is approved by the governor in council. The concession is granted only if in the opinion of the governor in council-and I quote from the section:
(a)	Drilling the oil well is desirable in order to extend the patroluem resources of Canada; and
(b)	The taxpayer could not reasonably be expected to drill the oil well unless permitted to deduct at least fifty per centum of the expenditures in connection therewith from tax.
What that means, of course, is that if the well is successful, half the cost is paid by the people of Canada, and that is a substantial concession. The government felt that, offered once, it should not be extended to renewing operations in the same well. I should correct my statement and say that if the well is successful the taxpayer does bear the cost, but if it is a loss the taxpayers of Canada do bear half the cost of the drilling expenses.

In my opinion the reasons which the minister has just read are the very ones which should cause this tax concession to be extended to abandoned exploratory wells. As he said, the sole idea of the tax concession is to encourage drilling, and if possible to develop new fields. In many instances these abandoned exploratory wells are the very ones which we might expect to bring in new fields. I can see no reason in the world why these wells should be cut off from this concession.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Obviously it is a matter on which opinions may differ. The purpose is to encourage the drilling of new wells. The incentive should not be greater than what is believed to be necessary to accomplish that

purpose. It is felt that the cost of deepening an existing well is not as great as the cost of starting and drilling one down to a certain depth. These wells must be deep test wells, and not the ordinary shallow well. I speak on this with some diffidence in reply to my hon. friend, because I know he is much more familiar with the practical details of oil mining operations than I am, but he also knows that under the subsection the enterprise is one w'hich must be approved by the Minister of Mines and Resources. These are special cases.

So far as the Department of Finance is concerned the chief difficulty is that there is no real understanding of the oil business and what is necessary to encourage an increased oil production. The only way in which you can get people to put money in as risky a business as drilling for oil is to make it reasonably possible that they will get some sort of return. Unless some form of tax concession is made we are going to have the situation continue which prevails in Alberta at the present time, with the majority of the drilling rigs sitting idle and nothing going on. It is time that the Department of Finance realized that the present tax structure is stifling oil exploration.
I was particularly disappointed to hear the minister say that no further tax concessions were in prospect in view of the concessions which were made to the mining industry. The very least that might be done is to increase the depletion allowance from 33% per cent to 50 per cent, which would bring it in line with the depletion allowance allowed in the United States, and would bring it partly in line with the concessions now made to mining enterprises.
So far as the subsidies are concerned, there are one or two other things I should like to say-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, I pointed out that subsidies do not come under this resolution. Under this resolution we are not granting subsidies. They come under another item in the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I really do not want to interrupt my hon. friend, but I am "not prepared to deal with the question of subsidies to the oil industry to-day. I have not the information with me; I am not in a position to answer my hon. friend now, and I do urge that he raise this matter at the proper time, when I shall be very glad to discuss it. Then I will have the necessary data either to agree with or to differ from him, but I have not the information and am not in a position to discuss it to-day. I have no doubt the statements he is making are correct, but I feel they should be made when I can answer them and give an explanation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Since the matter of subsidies comes under a different item I think it should be discussed when that item is reached.

While it may come under a different item, the point is that it is actually oil taxation, and it is so closely related to this item that it seemed to me this was the proper time to say something about it. However, that is the situation. It is a form of hidden taxation on the oil industry, and having made the point I shall leave it at that.
As far as section 31 itself is concerned, I wonder if the minister could state in simple words what the thing means, because as I read it, it appears that the oil industry is going to be worse off than before. My understanding having been in touch with the officials of the department, is that the industry is going to be in exactly the same position as in previous years. I should like a little clarification as to exactly what this section means and how it will work out in a specific case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall do the best I can, Mr. Chairman. The only change from the law as it exists at present and as it has existed for several years is that the percentage rate is reduced from 26J per cent to 20 per cent and from 40 per cent to 30 per cent; and those changes are merely consequential upon the reduction in the rate of corporation income tax which is being made and which has to be made by reason of the undertaking to the provinces under the tax agreements. I am
advised the effect is a one hundred per cent write-off. I do not know whether that is clear to my hon. friend.

No; what the minister means by a one hundred per cent write-off is not clear at all. My understanding from what he has said and the information I obtained before is that the oil industry has had no tax relief, that it is in exactly the same position as before the budget was brought down. An ordinary corporation has had a reduction in the corporation tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It shares in the general tax reduction, along with everybody else.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They are reduced in the same proportion; he gets the same reduction he had before. As expressed in terms of percentages it is lower, but that is because the tax rates are lower; and, as I said a moment ago, this is equivalent to a one hundred per cent write-off. If my hon. friend will take my assurance on that point, I am relying upon the assurance of my officials, who I know are thoroughly familiar with the circumstances. The hon. member might care to study this when we have the bill before us. When he sees the specific terms of the amendment, if he is still in doubt I shall be glad to elaborate what I am saying now, but I do give him the assurance that the position is exactly the same, that the percentage rate of tax reduction is merely consequential upon the reduction in the tax rate, and that the effect is a one hundred per cent write-off.

Could I .put the thing in this way, then? Take an oil company which paid taxes of $50,000 last year. What tax are they going to pay this year, if their business is the same? What reduction is there, if any?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Well, from my hon. friend's hypothetical question I assume that the $50,000 represented 40 per cent of a certain taxable income. This year they will pay 30 per cent of that taxable income. I cannot make the calculation at once, but it is merely an arithmetical problem. They will pay 30 per cent of that same taxable income.

I confess I am not quite clear yet as to what the minister meant by saying it was equivalent to a one hundred per cent write-off; and while

I am on my feet I want to ask another question. The minister said plainly and categorically that this was incentive legislation. By that I understand that it is an inducement, that it is to induce people to take certain action, in this case to produce oil. Then I want to ask the minister if he accepts the statement made by the hon. member for Calgary East that the majority of the rigs are idle. If that is so, and the statement was not questioned, does it not make it appear that the incentive is not working, and does not that raise the question whether or not the government do in fact want these rigs to be operating? If they do, should they not consider whether, as I say, in fact the incentive is sufficient?
speakername: Mr.   M A CD ON N ELL@Muskoka-Ontario

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If I have understood my hon. friend's question correctly, he puts it on this basis, that because there are idle rigs the incentive perhaps is not adequate.
The statement made by my hon. friend was that a majority of the rigs are idle. I speak in ignorance of the facts.
speakername: Mr.   M A CD ON N ELL@Muskoka-Ontario

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: So do I; I do not know whether they are or not.
Nevertheless we have here a witness who I submit for this purpose is an expert, whose evidence has not been challenged; and he says-
speakername: Mr.   M A CD ON N ELL@Muskoka-Ontario

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Let us call him an advocate as well as a witness.

All right; I will not quarrel with that. At any rate this statement has not been questioned ; I accept it, and I imagine the minister accepts it also. If that is correct, and the majority of the rigs are idle, is it not fair to ask the minister whether his incentive is working, whether some explanation is not required to make this clause appear reasonable?
speakername: Mr.   M A CD ON N ELL@Muskoka-Ontario

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
All I can say is that the government has no desire to go into the oil business. The rigs may be idle from a variety of causes. I do not know whether my hon. friend's statement is a complete picture or not, but I repeat what I have said previously. This is incentive legislation. These special concessions to the oil industry are matters which have been threshed out, worked out and discussed in this house year after year. There has been no change for the last two or three years. It may be that there should be greater incentive given, I do not know; that is a matter of opinion, but the government has come to the conclusion that this is not the
year to do so. My own view is that further incentive is not needed; that is my personal opinion.

The reason we are taking up your time this morning is that we hope to convince you that you are wrong, however faint that hope may be. The minister said the government did not want to get into the oil business. I did not understand that remark at all, because it did not seem to me to be relevant to the very strong statement the minister made before, that this was incentive legislation. I still submit the minister -has left the question entirely unanswered, because if this is incentive legislation, I understand that to mean the government has decided that it does want oil produced in Alberta.
speakername: Mr.   M A CD ON N ELL@Muskoka-Ontario

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: By the other fellow, and not at too great a price.

Wait a moment. If I understand incentive legislation it is intended to produce certain results, and again I submit that we have the minister's statement that this legislation is intended to produce results; we have the statement of the hon. member for Calgary East that it is not producing results, so I submit with deference -that it is up to the government to reconsider the discussions which have taken place in the last few years, because after all some very important people were not present here during those discussions.
speakername: Mr.   M A CD ON N ELL@Muskoka-Ontario

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is quite true.

I do not think there can be any question that wells are not being drilled to the extent that they might be. True, a certain number are being drilled, but there is no full drilling programme in operation, or a programme anything like there should be. As a matter of fact when I came to Ottawa to attend the sitting of parliament, twenty-eight out of thirty-two large drilling rigs in the Turner valley were sitting idle, and I am informed that condition still prevails. Most people who own probable drilling sites, and a large number -who have money enough to go ahead with the- drilling of wells, cannot see sufficient possibility of a return, under the present tax structure, and particularly in view of the subsidy which operates as an artificial depression of price to the extent of 75 cents a barrel, to go ahead with drilling.
This morning I was talking to a man who has an intimate knowledge of the oil business. The company with which he is connected has fifteen possible drilling sites. Those sites will at some time be drilled in t-he Turner valley, but they are not going to drill any of them

Income War Tax
until we get rid of the subsidy, or the tax situation is much improved so they can get a reasonable return from the oil for their shareholders. They believe it is much better to leave it in the ground than to take it out at the present time, because by taking it out they would simply be depleting their assets. It will be understood that once oil is taken from, the ground, the well is exhausted. Under the present circumstances they are much happier to leave the oil in the ground than to go into production. This is true of most of the oil companies.
Mr, ZAPLITNY: I admit at once that-I am no more an oil expert than is the minister, but I must say I am at a loss to understand what the hon. member for Calgary East is advocating. It seems to me he is admitting that no drilling is taking place, even though certain companies have sites, money and drilling equipment, simply because the return they believe they could expect will not be as great as they should like to have it. He also advocates removal of the subsidy and an increase in the price. I cannot see the logic in that, because it seems to me the whole reason for the subsidy has been to keep the price down in the west. We had an example of that earlier this year-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I objected to the hon. member for Calgary East discussing subsidies, and I feel I must do the same when the hon. member for Dauphin proceeds to do so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would call the attention of the hon. member for Dauphin to the fact that an arrangement was made under which subsidies would not be discussed at this time. That comes under another item.

My only reason for bringing it up was that it had already been brought into the discussion. However, if it is the wish of the committee, I shall desist. I would say this, however, that a while ago the minister pointed out that the government did not wish to go into the oil business. If what the hon. member for Calgary East says is true-and I have no reason to doubt it-I am quite sure the government eventually will have to get into the oil business, to produce oil. It is admitted that certain of these companies have sites, money and equipment, but they will not drill for oil unless they are assured of a certain return. That is not private enterprise. Certainly it is not true private enterprise.

Apparently the hon.
member for Dauphin does not understand the situation at all.
You explain it, then.

I do not believe he or anybody else would put money into an enterprise the resources of which were being exhausted, unless he could see some reasonable return on his capital, let alone to make any profit. That is essentially the situation. Under ordinary circumstances any enterprise is capable of operating at a loss for only a relatively short time before it goes broke. That is what has happened to many of the oil companies. Those which are still in operation and have drilling sites see no reason in the world why they should drill, spend a lot of money, and perhaps not even get a well, unless they have a reasonable return. But if they do get a well, they do not receive sufficient return to recoup themselves for the money they put into it.

I believe the hon. member for Calgary East has made a strong case for greater consideration of these companies which endeavour to bring more oil to the surface, so that we shall have a better supply of domestic oil for use in the west. The oil we buy from the United States requires payment of a 75-cent subsidy to get it here. One would conclude, therefore, that the Canadian price is 75 cents below the world or United States price, or the price which is considered necessary to get oil from the well-developed fields just across the border from our western provinces. It would therefore seem clear, even to one without great experience in this field, that the price in Canada is not sufficient to encourage drilling, or to encourage the supply of domestic oil. I should think that, with the government's other measures to protect our supply of United States exchange, it would do everything in its power to bring more Canadian oil to the surface, so that we should not have to buy in the United States, much less pay the 75-cent subsidy above the Canadian price in order to bring the oil here.
Undoubtedly the industry is a particularly hazardous one. I believe the present allowances do not go as far as they might to encourage production. Those allowances should be increased. While I do not wish to mention the subsidy again, yet it is so germane to the subject matter that it must be apparent to all hon. members that our oil producers are in a much more hazardous field than are the producers in the United States field across the border. Yet they do not get the price those producers get. At the same time we are not giving our producers as fair an increase in the depletion allowance as we should, in order to encourage them, especially
Income War Tax

when they have to work under a price level substantially lower than that which applies in the United States. Therefore I stand behind the suggestion made by the hon. member for Calgary East, in the hope that the government will give consideration to the fact that our price is so much lower than that of imported oil. If some relief can be given, through increased depletion allowance and tax drawback on the wells which are drilled, as well as the deep test wells, we shall greatly improve the Canadian economy and save United States exchange.

I am sorry to -be so persistent when the minister is so gracious; nevertheless I still think we are in a very unsatisfactory position, and I hope the minister will have another look at it.
I wish to make one comment on what the hon. member for Dauphin has said. He pointed out that people who were in this business wanted to be assured of a return. I think we ought to try to speak accurately-and I think the hon. member does try. I believe if he will study the situation he will find that there is enough money lost to satisfy either him or anybody else who feels that those who are in private enterprise should make losses. I think he will find that there are plenty of losses.

speechtext: The position with respect to tax concessions to the oil industry can be summarized in this way. In the first place, the treasury bears 50 per cent of the cost of drilling unsuccessful deep test wells. Second, every oil company is allowed to write off the capital cost against profit and loss.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The proposal of the government goes further than that, so far as incentive legislation is concerned. We will pay up to 50 per cent of the cost of drilling an unsuccessful deep test well. If the well is successful I assume that the operator would get back one hundred per cent of his cost. That is as far as the government felt it could properly go in the line of incentive legislation-. That judgment may be mistaken, but there are other reasons which result in failure to drill wells. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has pointed out that he helped to finance the first successful oil well in the Turner valley. One of the greatest incentives to further drilling is the bringing in of a new well. The hon. member for Calgary East knows that as well as I. As I have said, the government feels that the present incentives are all that it can afford to offer under existing conditions.

I think the minister is under a misapprehension when he states that the treasury bears fifty per cent of the cost of an unsuccessful deep test well. If a new company starts out in the oil drilling business and drills a deep test well, it gets nothing whatever from the treasury. The only case in which the treasury bears fifty per cent of the cost is where a well is drilled by a company having sufficient revenue. I think I can make my point clear by a simple example. If it costs, say $400,000, to drill a deep test well, and it proves to be a dry hole, a small company with an income of $100,000 per year from producing wells would get a tax concession of $19,000 on their $400,000 loss. In other words, they would have a loss in connection with drilling that well of $381,000. If the well was drilled by a large company with an income of $1,000,000 from producing wells, the tax concession on that particular well would be $190,000. In other words it would, cost that company $210,000 to drill the well. As you can readily see, the effect of this will be to discourage new capital. There is no incentive in this resolution for new capital to go into the oil business. There are several small companies in Calgary which have drilling rigs and the necessary money, but they know that if they spend from $300,000 to $600,000 on a deep test well they will get no help from the government under this resolution. They would lose their money and would be out of business. Considering the return that they would get if they did bring in a producing well, they decide not to drill at all.

The only people that this legislation really helps are the large companies. One of my objections to it is that it does not encourage the small operator who is chiefly responsible for bringing in new oil fields. Once a field has been discovered the large companies come in and buy up the various leases and drill wells, but in most cases the new wells which have been discovered on this continent were discovered by the wild-catter who puts down a well at times in places where the geologists say there would be no use in putting one down. That is how the great oil development has taken place throughout this country. This legislation does not help the small man.

From the point of view of capitalism I think the hon. member who has just taken his seat- has made a good point. Undoubtedly the smaller men are at a disadvantage, but if the government is going to bonus this industry I suggest it should bonus itself and take either the loss or the gain, as the case may be, and not just go out to bonus every Tom, Dick, and Harry who may want to go into the oil business.

There is no question of the government bonusing the industry. What the industry is asking for is a fair deal in the matter of taxes. Then it is asking for an extension of this fifty per cent provision on deep test wells to wells which are drilled in the plains area. I do not know why the government will not put that into effect, because an oil well that goes down two or three thousand feet is just as valuable to the country as one that goes down 40,000 feet. As far as present exploration goes it looks as though there might be a better chance, in the next two or three years, of developing oil wells in the plains than in the foothills area. speechtext:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
While the minister is
getting the data with respect to production, I wonder if he would try to get a little further information. I am concerned with seeing that the Canadian people have a correct view with respect to the oil industry in Canada, and not a wrong view. If other taxpayers in Canada are not bonusing this industry, it is time we knew it, and time we knew that any other impression is not correct. The minister has said-and we accept his statement-that the oil industry has not been a burden upon the people, except to the extent that general surveys and work of that type along basic lines has been done. In addition to its not being any burden on the taxpayers of Canada, this industry has been of some advantage in providing employment and revenue from taxation to carry on the ordinary activities of government. All hon. members
will have access to the ordinary statistics of employment, but perhaps the minister could give us some idea of what the oil industry has contributed by way of taxation to the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I think perhaps I can get information on that which would be of interest. Of course my hon. friend will appreciate that the oil industry, like a great many other industries, is divided into a number of compartments. There are marketing companies, companies which operate here in the east, some of which have nothing whatever to do with the production of oil. They have the crude oil refined and distributed as gasoline and lubricating oils. Others do not even do that; they simply buy gasoline and sell it. They are nothing more or less than retailers.
I take it my hon. friend's question relates principally to the industry so far as it engages in the production of oil in Canada. If that is correct I shall see what figures I can get and give them to the committee at another time. Perhaps the appropriate time would be when we are in committee on second reading of the bill. However I shall get what I can.

In order to keep the record straight, not only have the oil producers of Canada not been a burden on the taxpayers, but they have saved the taxpayers between $5 million and $10 million a year in the past several years in subsidies which would otherwise have been paid. I am not returning to the matter of subsidies, but I am simply pointing out the way in which that amount of money was saved to the Canadian taxpayer.

And on exchange in
respect of oil coming into Canada.

Yes, as the hon. member for Davenport says, on exchange. In addition, the oil producers for some time have bonused consumers of gasoline and oil products in western Canada to a greater extent than that. The bonus to consumers in western Canada last year was about $8 million. It is impossible for me to say definitely how much the oil producers saved the country, or how much they bonused the oil consumer, because the government has seen fit to withhold from me any information as to subsidies paid. However, through private sources I have found out that the subsidy was about 75 cents a barrel -indeed in some cases it amounted to 80 cents.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We are right back on subsidies again.

That would be a rough estimate of the amount of money the tax-
Income War Tax

payers have been saved by the oil producers, and the extent to which the oil producers have bonused the consumer.

If the minister is going to produce figures to show the position of producing oil companies, and if he wishes to paint a fair picture, he should also produce the figures for the closely allied handling companies. Their directorates in some instances are interlocking. To paint a fair picture of the oil industry he would have to show not only the profits made by the producing companies, but also those made by the handling, distributing and pipeline companies.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I pointed out to the leader of the opposition that he had given a fairly big order, but I promised to do the best I could. I shall consider the hon. member's request. It will be recognized, though, that to make a complete and analytical survey of the oil industry in all its ramifications-although a good' deal of the information may be available in the bureau of statistics-would be a large order, I might be able to get it before September or October when the house rises.

I have followed carefully the remarks of my leader, of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and of other hon. members of this party. I believe the committee recognizes that there are few industries more indigenous to Canada than the oil industry. I observe with interest and some concern the fall of our oil production.
In reply to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario the minister said he thought this condition was worth another look. Before that he had indicated that there was very little probability of the government changing its mind.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This year.

Yes, this year. Of course governments often change their minds, even when front-rank members of the cabinet are in doubt. Sometimes I have seen cabinet ministers change their minds when other cabinet ministers did not know they were changing. Recently the Prime Minister changed his mind when none of the cabinet knew he was changing it. So I still think there may be hope. I suggest the minister carry out his undertaking to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and let the section stand in order that he may have another look at it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
If the committee insists that it stand I shall have to comply, but I do ask that it be permitted to pass. There will be another opportunity for discussion when the bill is presented. I hesitate to 
interject a personal note, but I have a heavy programme to place before the house. I indicated earlier that I thought there was no reasonable possibility of our making any substantial change in the oil tax programme this year. Of course if the committee insists I shall have to allow the resolution to stand. But there is no change this year, and I think I ought to ask the committee to permit it to pass. I could consider it between now and the time the bill is presented.

I understood the minister to say he thought it was unfair that he should take another look at the situation, and I thought his answer indicated there might be a slight chance. However, in view of what the minister has said I shall not insist that any change be made. I do express my regret that the government has not seen fit to leave the incentive as it has been.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We are leaving it exactly as it it; there is no change.
I mean that I regret there has been no increase in the incentive.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We are just continuing for another year provisions which have been in force for three years.

The government could very well have given consideration to increasing the incentive, and I regret that the only incentive given is that which can be taken out of profits already earned. There is no incentive offered to companies which might not have any profit. The government would be well-advised in my opinion-if it is in power in another year-to increase the incentive, because I know of nothing more important at the present time than the oil industry. It is regrettable to think that production has fallen.

I shall give one brief example to encourage the minister to stick to any programme which would develop the oil industry. The development of that industry in the area around Norman Wells in the far north has resulted in a brand new business down here in this part of the country. It has been found that the burning of the fuel oil produced in that country encourages people in the far north to invest money in the building of houses which, because of the high price of coal up there, would not otherwise be built. There is no wood available for fuel purposes up there. The development of oil at Norman Wells has been a mighty fine thing, because it has brought about a new industry to manufacture stoves and furnaces to burn oil for use in the north country. This is just one small example of the benefits

Income War Tax
brought about in increased employment created by investments by this and other governments in promoting the production of oil. Still further examples might be created and more employment, created. I am told it is possible that thousands of these oil stoves will be required. I should like my hon. friends to my left, for whom I have a high regard, to try to get that point of view and realize the results that can be obtained by the country making these investments in prospecting. I am not making any comment upon whether it is or is not enough; I am simply grateful for anything the government can do to develop our resources and provide employment, not only in the west but in the plants of Ontario and Quebec.

speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.

That the deduction from tax allowed to a corporation, association, syndicate or exploration partnership formed for the purpose of exploring and drilling for oil in respect of exploration and drilling expenses be extended to expenditures incurred during the year 1947 but that in respect of expenditures in that year the deductions be reduced from 26jf per cent to 20 per cent thereof.
What is the essential difference between resolution 32 and1 resolution 31?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Resolution 32 is for the
benefit of new companies which do not have an income. It will enable them to carry axploration expenses forward and deduct them if and when they do have an income. It is the same as the law now stands.

I thought the clause was to apply to new companies, particularly syndicates and partnerships which might be set up for the purpose of drilling for oil. I would assume that this resolution 32 applies particularly to what you would term the small man; that it was meant to apply to him.

speechtext: Not necessarily.
It applies more to him than to the large corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I do not know that I
would agree with that.
Why is the clause which appears in 31 "the deepening of oil wells which is completed in 1947" left out of 32?

speechtext:
This is to cover an exploration enterprise, not a deep test well. The provisions covering deep test wells are to be found in another resolution. They must be approved by the Department of Mines and Resources and be authorized by the governor 63260-267

I am not suggesting that either of these resolutions has to do with deep test wells. I was simply asking the essential difference between 32 and 31. I then asked why that did not contain the clause, "the deepening of oil wells which is completed in 1947" which is included in 31.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This and other resolutions are drafted in broad general terms, and when my hon. friend looks at the legislation I think he will find that it covers the point he has in mind.

Resolution 31 provides for a reduction in deductions from 26} per cent and 40 per cent to 20 per cent and 30 per cent respectively, whereas 32 only allows for a reduction from 26} per cent to 20 per cent. Why is not the 40 per cent and 30 per cent included in the resolution?

speechtext:
Presumably the new company which was formed would not be an oil marketing company. There are two types of companies, as my friend knows, the oil marketing company and the purely producing company. The rates are different, depending upon whether it is an oil marketing company or a producing company, or there might be a combination of both.
Mr. HARKNESS1: Is the minister suggesting that the oil marketing company should have a greater allowance than the straight oi'l producing or searching company? That would seem to be the effect of what he is saying.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

What type of company would be affected if resolution 32 were dropped?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: A new enterprise formed for the purpose of exploring for oil.
They would not be covered by 31?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
They are not really covered by 31. Als I explained a moment ago, 32

allows an accumulation of exploration expenses to be used in a subsequent year when there may be profits. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
10. That for the 1947 and subsequent taxation years, a corporation other than a corporation whose income is primarily obtained from mining or logging operations shall not be allowed to deduct from income any corporation tax as defined in the existing wartime tax agreements paid to the government of a province.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Resolutions 10 and 11
arise out of the dominion offer to provincial governments regarding tax fields. Resolution 10 states generally that provincial corporation taxes will not be allowed as a deduction in computing profits for purposes of the dominion corporation income tax. The exception to this general rule is the taxes levied on corporations whose income is primarily obtained from mining or logging operations. Resolution 11 makes positive provision for the deduction of taxes on profits levied by provincial governments on income from mining or logging operations. As the committee is aware, taxes on profits are not ordinarily regarded as an expense of doing business, and accordingly in the absence of any specific provision such taxes would not be deductible. Under this provision however the effect will be that the dominion corporation income tax will apply to the profit remaining after provincial governments have levied their taxes on profits from mining and logging operations.
I should correct, I think, at this time a misunderstanding of the purpose of resolu-

Income War Tax
tions 10 and 11 which appears to have arisen. In the budget debate on July 8 the hon. member for Nanaimo implied that under the dominion-provincial proposals these industries were being singled out for double taxation. It should be clear now, I think, to the hon. member that the purpose of these resolutions is to * give relief from double taxation where it exists in the mining and logging fields. If special taxes are levied on these industries by provincial governments, as is the case in one province at least, relief will be obtainable under resolution 11 now to be proposed.
But they still can be taxed both by the dominion government and by a provincial or municipal government if a provincial or municipal government so desires.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct, but, contrary to the general rule, in the case of these companies the dominion government will allow as a deduction from income the tax, if any, paid to a provincial government-which has never been done in the past.
Are we on resolution 10?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We are on No. 10. I dealt with 10 and 11 together because they are closely allied.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
11. That there be allowed as a deduction from income earned after January 1, 1947, of a corporation whose income is primarily obtained from mining or logging operations taxes paid by it to the government of any province including income tax on income earned after January 1, 1947.

I have an amendment. I will read the amendment first.
That there be allowed as a deduction from income earned after January 1, 1947, of a corporation whose income or on that part of such income which is primarily obtained from mining or logging operations taxes paid by it to the government of any province including income tax on income earned after January il, 1947.
The new words are "or on that part of such income." I suggest that for this reason, that there are companies whose primary business may not be logging or mining but whose interests contain a mine-particularly I am thinking of a mine. We will take a steel company operating a mine: the primary business of that corporation would be the manufacture of steel-at least we hope it is going to be the manufacture of steel, shortly-but because its primary function is the manufacture of steel it would not come in under and get the benefit of this clause. Nevertheless it is operating a mine. There are one or two corporations in that class, and I have 63260-267i
suggested that the seven words be added to the resolution to cover such cases. It does not alter the resolution at all, but merely allows companies of the kind I have mentioned to come under the clause.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I would be ready to accept the amendment. The intention is that the tax on that particular kind of income will be treated as a deduction, regardless of what type of company it is, and that will be made clear in the legislation. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendment would enlarge the class of those who would obtain benefits.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think not, Mr. Chairman. I indicated that it was really our intention to include incomes such as my hon. friend has suggested'. I believe myself that the resolution is probably wide enough to cover what he has in mind, but to make it perfectly clear I am ready to allow those words to be inserted. I do not take the stand that it. enlarges the purpose of the resolution. I believe the resolution covers the point now. However, I accept the amendment in order to satisfy the oommit.tee. The legislation will unquestionably make the point perfectly clear, and if my hon. friend is prepared to take that assurance it will meet the situation. It is on the record now. The legislation will include the provision, but if he prefers to have the resolution in the form he has suggested I have no objection.
If it is all the same to the minister, I am speaking of matters such as royalties paid on a fee basis to the province.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am satisfied that the amendment does not enlarge the purpose of the resolution, but is for the purpose of clarification, and therefore I accept it.
Thank you veTy much.

Before the clause as amended is carried I would like to read to the minister portions of a letter from a mining company in my constituency showing the seriousness of the loss incurred by mining companies as a result of putting the Canadian dollar on a parity with that of the United States. I quote:
The proposal of the government to allow a depletion of $2 an ounce as an alternative to the 33J per cent of profits is of no relief whatever to this company, along with most other established operators.
Income War Tax

The loss of $3.50 an ounce caused by bringing our dollar to parity with that of the States is a very serious one to us. Labour and other costs have gone up greatly, and are going higher. Unless some relief is found, either by way of an increase in the price of gold, reduced taxation, or increase of the depletion allowance on profits to a very substantial degree, our marginal operations such as that on Bonanza Creek will have to be shut down, and our proposed development programme will halt.
I hope the minister will find some way of remedying that situation, in regard to mining companies, gold mining companies particularly, which provide such a large amount of employment for men in Canada, and which spend so much in the purchase of supplies and equipment. Their plight is not a pleasant one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
My hon. friend was kind enough to send me a copy of the letter to which he has referred, and I appreciate that the change in the exchange value has had important consequences for every gold mining company. The statement I made in the house last Friday evening, I believe it was, sets out the utmost the government feels it can do under existing circumstances to help to correct that situation to some extent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
This resolution relates to the three-year averaging for farmers and fishermen. The resolution, after being considered by the committee on Thursday, July 25, was allowed to stand, and I undertook to give further consideration to the representations made by various hon. members in connection with it. The main point urged at that time was that for averaging on a five-year rather than on p, three-year basis. In the meantime I have considered carefully the arguments put forward by hon. members, and at the same time have considered other aspects of the proposal. I think the committee will agree that the proposal for a moving three-year average meets to a large extent the claims for a longer period of averaging. This aspect of the proposal was, I believe, emphasized fully the other day.
The second point, which I think was not perhaps fully appreciated in the previous discussion of the item, was that if a five-year rather than a three-year average is taken, farmers and fishermen would obtain no benefit from the provision until five years hence. This seems to be an important consideration in favour of the three-year rather than the five-year period. In the discussion of the item the

other afternoon it was pointed out several times that the administration of income tax with respect to farmers is not easy because of accounting difficulties and lack of adequate records. To those advocating the five-year averaging, I must point out the difficult requirements imposed on farmers in keeping adequate records. The introduction of this principle of averaging is a completely new departure in the income tax system, and is proposed here for one group of income taxpayers. I regard the three-year average as substantially meeting the requests of industry, and for the reasons stated above I have concluded that the original proposal for a three-year moving average is, on balance, a practicable method and represents a satisfactory alleviating measure.
'Resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This is related to the question of service pay and allowances. I believe the main part of the discussion had reference to the income tax treatment of certain special income tax groups, including particularly the fire-fighters.
And auxiliary services.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes. I have given careful consideration to the representations which were made by various members in the course of the discussion. As I pointed out at the time, it was not a new subject to me, but one which I had been in fairly close touch with for at least three years. I stated the general principle on which, the government had proceeded1 in connection with income tax exemptions for these groups, namely that it had never been considered desirable or appropriate to grant complete income tax exemption to any civilian group. The question of certain special benefits for the fire fighters and auxiliary services, I believe, is the subject of legislation which was considered by the veterans affairs committee and which will be before the house in a few days. On the question of income tax exemption, the question so far as the auxiliary services is concerned was settled some time ago by order in council, and I believe the members of the committee are familiar with the basis on

Income War Tax
which that matter was disposed of. When I spoke the other day I indicated that I thought special provision had been made, or was being made, for the fire fighters. At the time I spoke I was not aware that an order in council had been passed dealing with that question as well. The position under the order in council is that the fire fighters are being treated substantially on the same basis as the auxiliary services. I am advised that remission of taxes payable for 1942 in respect of pay and allowances, including dependents' allowances, while serving outside the western hemisphere, has been granted on the ground that no deductions were made and that they were not aware that they were taxable. For subsequent years the basis of the remission of taxes is granted in respect of one-fifth of service pay and allowances, including dependents' allowances for 1943, 1944, and 1945 during which, they served outside the western hemisphere. There is also remission of the refundable portion of the tax calculated for all the years from 1942 to 1945 inclusive. I am informed that that is comparable to the bases on which the auxiliary services were treated. I do not know that there is anything more I can add, except to say that after consideration by myself and my colleagues we feel that complete exemption cannot be granted.
I am getting figures which were asked for by some hon. members as to how many are involved. Apparently 422 persons were involved in all, of whom twenty-nine were officers and 393 other ranks. I refer now to the fire fighters. The first of such personnel went overseas in May, 1942. The whole corps was overseas by December, 1942, and they returned to Canada in 1945. As to whether any have paid taxes, the information is not available, but it is anticipated that across Canada some may have done so. Since the T-4 information as a check was not available, it has not been possible to say as yet how many have been assessed. There was no deduction of taxes at the source for these individuals, the table of tax deductions not having been sent outside of Canada. It is probably fair to say that as a result of the remissions to which I have referred the vast majority of these persons would not come within the tax category.
The fire fighters?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes. The deputy minister advises me that in effect the provision which has been made here will result in complete tax exemption for over ninety per cent of those involved. As to the auxiliary services, I have not any estimate as to that. I should think they might be on a somewhat different basis.
The contention of those of us who pressed for the complete exemption was that all these men were in effect the same as men in the armed forces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I appreciate that.

And should be treated in the same way. I have no intention to-day of repeating the arguments, but that is what we believe, and we certainly are not satisfied with the statement the minister has just made.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I appreciate the fact that that was the position my hon. friend took. In the previous discussion he made that clear, including the reasons which led him to put forward that view. I say with regret that we have not been able to accept it.
What is the position of the civilian employees of the Canadian Legion Educational Services so far as tax remission for the war years is concerned?

speechtext: If serving overseas they are considered as forming part of this auxiliary service to which I have referred, and they were granted a tax exemption with respect to one-fifth of their pay, dependents' allowances, subsistence allowances and the like, and the refundable portion of their tax was remitted along the same lines as I indicated a moment ago with respect to these fire fighters.
That is now final.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is final so far as anything is final in this world.

The other evening I asked the minister why the fire fighters had not been taxed at the source. A few moments ago he indicated that the tables had not been sent out of Canada, or something to that effect. They were not taxed at the source, but I understood that the supervisors were; therefore the tax tables of the supervisors must have left Canada.

speechtext: My hon. friend may be right. The supervisors were in a somewhat different position from the fire fighters. As my hon. friend knows, the joint service organization in Ottawa had headquarters here. They were in close touch with army headquarters all the time, and it may be that there was a little better liaison with that group than with some others, but I would not be prepared to say that the hon. member is not correct in what he has just said.

In cases where the tax of these auxiliary groups was not paid while they were overseas, what steps are customarily taken to secure the tax in arrears? It is going
Income War Tax

to be a little bit of a blow on quite a few pocketbooks.

speechtext:
The procedure is the
ordinary collection of accounts method. As the hon. member for Regina City says, it may come as an expensive surprise. I do not know that I can elaborate on the answer.

The department has the
collection machinery.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The deputy minister assures me that in the Department of National Revenue he has an efficient collection machine.

be repealed.
Is the minister going to explain?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This resolution has already been discussed at length. It is one of the three resolutions which refer to the armed services and the merchant marine. The only questions we were discussing were in relation to the auxiliary sendees, the fire fighters and the like. I do not think there is anything further, unless my hon. friend has some point he should like to raise. I thought we had pretty well covered the general discussion and were concentrating on the question of these special groups.
That is not my recollection of the discussion which took place.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is all right.

We had not got any farther than a discussion on resolution 18. There are still some points which I should like to raise in connection with resolution 19, which deals with an entirely different class of people, namely, citizens, soldiers, sailors

and airmen who gave up their spare time in order to prepare themselves for the defence of their country. I can understand the reasoning as applied to the regular soldier, sailor and airman, that the income which he derives from his pay and allowances is his main source of income. Soldiering or his work in the service is his life profession, but those gentlemen who are in the non-permanent militia are giving up their spare time. Any pay and allowances which they draw cannot be regarded as their regular source of income. These men of all ranks in the past have drawn on an average, I should say, about fifteen days' pay ini a year. I believe the law limits the amount they can draw to thirty days' pay. Out of that pay it has been the custom in the past, and I do not suppose there is any radical change now, for officers, non-commissioned officers and men to contribute varying amounts to their regimental funds. In fact I do not think it is an exaggeration to say that in the long years between the first world war and the second world war, if it had not been for the contributions which were made by the personnel of the non-permanent militia we never would have been able to mobilize in the time w"e did when the second war broke out. I think credit for that speedy mobilization must be given to those citizens who devoted their time to this cause. It was not only their time; they devoted a large proportion of their pay and allowances as well. It was customary for officers of many units to contribute the whole of their pay. I will not say that was the universal practice, but it was done in a great many units. Sergeants contributed a large share of their pay, and the men of almost every unit made some contribution as well. It might have been only one day's pay of the fifteen; in some units the whole pay was put into the regimental fund, and these regimental funds enabled the units concerned to maintain their existence during the years between the wars, and to mobilize in 1939. Now these men are to be taxed on the amount of pay and allowances they receive. I should think it would be possible to make some exceptions. You might say that personnel who spend the whole summer in camp, serving on the staff, thereby drawing pay for perhaps two or three months as some of them have done in the past; personnel who take extended cruises on board ship; personnel who take courses lasting for two or three months, might reasonably be expected to pay income tax upon the amounts they draw. I do say, however, it is stretching the point too far to tax the civilian personnel on that fifteen days' pay, when a large portion of it is handed back.

Income War Tax
In the first place I would ask the minister to reconsider this matter and see if he could not except the ordinary day's pay and allowances for the ordinary training. If he will not go that far, will he not allow as a deduction such pay and allowances as are contributed to the regimental funds?
I should like to mention one other point. It must be remembered that many of the personnel have to buy uniforms and part of their equipment. The men you are now trying to encourage to go into the three services are young men just starting out in life. Many of them have not a great deal of money; and if they find themselves raised to a higher bracket for this reason it might be a deterrent, because after all the service is none too popular. The wives do not like to see these young men spending all their holidays in camp and going out evening after evening to train. As an encouragement to them I would ask the minister to consider first of all whether he cannot relieve them of the tax entirely on pay and allowances for normal training or, if not, at least allow contributions made to regimental funds as a deduction.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
First I thank my hon. and gallant friend for what he has said with respect to the work of the reserve army, with which I am in complete agreement. On this question of tax exemption, I think he was here the other night and probably heard my views in that regard. I am against tax exemptions. I do not think there should be any. If we were granting them to any civilian group under circumstances such as the hon. member has outlined', probably the members of our reserve army who serve, as he has said, for a portion of their spare time during the year and perhaps go to camp for two or three weeks, would be a deserving case; but I do not think we can grant complete exemption to any class.
On the other point, I am advised that contributions by members of the reserve army to regimental funds are properly deductible from income for tax purposes. That does not include contributions to the officers' mess, of course, or for special comforts for one group, but donations made by anyone to regimental funds, particularly in the case-as I know it is the case-of officers and men who turn their pay in to the regimental funds, can be claimed as a deduction from income for purposes of taxation, of course up to ten per cent of a man's income, which I think would be adequate in most cases.
That would be ten per cent of his total income, not ten per cent of the pay and allowances?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Quite so. If a man had an income of $10,000 he could make donations up to $1,000.

I do not feel that I can add anything to what has been said so eloquently and logically by the hon. member for Nanaimo, but I should like to just second his remarks. I have had some experience with the militia; the Acting Minister of Finance is also Minister of National Defence, and I have no doubt his sympathies are entirely with what the hon. member has just stated.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I tried to make that clear.

I can assure the minister that he is going to have considerable trouble organizing the militia throughout this country if he puts handicaps such as this in the way. I know that before the war the officers did contribute practically all their pay either to the regimental fund or to the officers' mess. For many years they contributed part of their pay in order to help pay the men coming in. We were allowed only a skeleton company, and in order to increase the numbers the officers contributed part of their pay so that more men would be encouraged to go to camp. I must say I think it is a very short-sighted policy on the part of the government, when they are trying to build up the militia of this country, to impose upon themselves a handicap like this. I suggest that the minister carefully consider the recommendation which has been made by the hon. member for Nanaimo. I believe it would be beneficial indeed to the militia if it could be given favourable consideration.

I should like to support the suggestions advanced by the hon. member for Nanaimo and the hon. member for Royal. It is well understood by everyone who has had any experience with the nonpermanent militia that the money received in the form of pay and allowances is not real income. In most cases I believe the recipient of the pay and allowances is actually out of pocket at the end of the year as a result of his membership in the militia. In view of that fact I can hardly accept the minister's view that no exemptions or exceptions should be made. In many forms of business, money received which does not constitute real income, from the point of view of making the company any better off, is exempt; and it seems to me this is a proper case where an exemption should be made. As to the discouragement which the imposition of this tax causes among members of the militia and prospective members, I can give personal testimony. I know of two men in Calgary who served in the
Income War Tax

militia for many years, before the war and during the war, one of whom was overseas. Both were complaining bitterly about the fact that the pay and allowances they had received last year had worked in such a way as to bring their income a certain level, so they had a heavier tax imposed upon them. They not only spent the money which they had received as a result of being in the militia, but they were out the extra amount of money collected from them in taxes. I suggest that serious consideration be given the abolition of this tax.

Resolution agreed to.
20. That the exemption of amounts received by members of the merchant marine as war risk bonuses in respect of service in a war risk zone and of the value of board and lodging received on shipboard, while performing service in respect of which such bonuses are payable be repealed for 1947 and subsequent taxation years.

I should like to refer to
the manner in which merchant seamen who were interned have been treated. They have had to pay income tax for all the time they were interned. Apparently their money was held there by the government. A certain portion of it was used to help their dependents. The balance was retained, and some of it is still retained. Out of that balance these men are being assessed for income tax during the time they were in captivity. I suggest that is not a fair procedure. This matter was brought up in the veterans affairs committee, and the following unanimous recommendation was made in the report of that committee:
That income tax be remitted in respect of detention allowances payable to merchant seamen under the provisions of order in council P.C 12/4209 dated June 12, 1941, as amended by P.C. 87/5204 dated July 16. 1941.
It may be that resolution No. 20 is wide enough to enable the government to make the necessary provision in the bill. But if it is not, I would ask that the minister extend the terms of the resolution so that these men need not pay taxes for the time they were interned.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am advised that the matter is under sympathetic consideration. I do not know that I can make the positive statement at this time that it is being given favourable consideration. I am informed it is the type of special case which may be handled by remission under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, and I think that is the proper way to handle a special case of this kind on compassionate grounds. It is done in other eases, and I should think that this could be

handled in that way. I am glad my hon. friend has called my attention to it, and he can rest assured that it will receive sympathetic consideration.
Will the minister make a statement on the point when the bills are brought in?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I should hope I would have a chance to discuss it with the departmental officials before that time.
The discussion will be found at page 1472 of the proceedings of the veterans affairs committee.

Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I suggest that we take at this time the resolutions respecting the Excise Act, and then all resolutions can be reported at one time. We could take resolutions 1 and 2 together.
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Act and to provide:-
1.	That the excise duty of $3 per thousand on cigars be reduced to $1 per thousand.
2.	That any enactment founded on this resolution shall be deemed to have come into force on the twenty-eighth day of June, one thousand nine hundred and forty-six.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Under resolution 1 there is a reduction in the excise duty on cigars from S3 to $1 per thousand. This reduction may be considered along with the proposed amendment under the Special War Revenue Act, which I hope will be considered in a few minutes, and which repeals the present graduated specific tax on cigars, replacing it with a straight 25 per cent ad valorem tax. It is believed' that the new arrangement will be regarded as a fairer system than that which has been in effect. It will remove one of the awkward features of the existing system which repeatedly caused trouble. Under the present graduated tax an increase in selling price above certain points resulted in bringing on an additional tax far in excess of the increase in gross receipts resulting from the price increase. Under the straight ad valorem tax this so-called "notch problem" is eliminated. On balance the new arrangement with respect to taxes on cigars will produce slightly more revenue, possibly $160,000 or more a year.
Since the announcement in the budget of this tax change, various cigar manufacturers have requested that the new rate be only twenty per cent instead of the twenty-five per cent proposed. I have carefully considered these representations, but having regard

Excise Act
to the relative level of the taxes on cigars as compared with other forms of tobacco I do not consider that the twenty-five per cent tax is unreasonable. Accordingly I am not recommending that any change be made in the budget resolution.
In the latest fiscal year the revenue from cigars under the Special War Revenue Act and the Excise Act combined amounted to

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: When these resolutions were prepared, was serious and sympathetic consideration given to the removal of the tax of two cents a bottle on soft drinks? It seems to me that this is important, because it would help to give the young people of the country a greater opportunity of having small social gatherings-more than by reducing the tax on cigars.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We hope that this will produce an additional revenue of $160,000 a year.
They are only drugs, anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The tax to which my hon. friend refers comes under the Special War Revenue Act, which we will consider in a moment or two. He can ask his question at that time.
I believe this has been the cause of the elimination of the five-cent cigar. We now have to pay from fifteen to eighteen cents for two, or something of the kind.
How much does the minister expect to get in the way of revenue, as against the $2,240,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
As I indicated, we expect to get slightly more revenue, possibly as much as
S160,000	a year.

Although this question
may not fall directly under the resolutions before us, I would ask why it is that cigars went up in price. The six-eent cigar is now being sold at two for fifteen cents.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am advised that cigar manufacturers' costs, along with some other costs, have increased, and that they have, coincidentally with the change in taxes, adjusted their prices. As the committee knows, there is no ceiling on cigar prices.

Will the minister give a clearer explanation as to how much of the cost of a cigar is taken up in one or other of the two tax forms the minister has mentioned? With the tax being reduced from $3 to $1 per thousand I am confused when I am told that about $160,000 more will be received in revenue eaoh year, when it is combined with the ad valorem duty.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Because we are increasing the ad valorem tax.

W'hat is the tax on a cigar which sells wholesale at ten cents or fifteen cents? Cigar prices seem to have gone up twenty per cent, and while I believe this is a good place for a tax-I am all for it-the tax will increase the revenue by only about eight per cent', according to the estimate given by the departmental officials. I should like to understand it a little better.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know that I can give a definite answer. However, this is what it amounts to: the tax is $1 per thousand. My hon. friend is a better mathematician than I, and he can figure how much that would come to. Then there is 25 per cent of the selling price, which varies. I suppose the cigar manufacturer too pays his share of income tax.
The tax is now 25 per cent?

speechtext: Twenty-five per cent ad valorem and $1 per thousand excise.
