Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Special War Revenue Act and to provide:
1. That the securities transfer tax be extended to apply to rights to receive shares of stock.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This resolution relates to the securities transfer tax. Under the present provisions of the stock transfer tax, transfers of rights to receive shares of stock have not been taxable. The present resolution is that they shall be taxable in future. Hon. members who are familiar with matters in financial markets will know at once what is meant by dealing in rights. In a company reorganization or rearrangement of the capital set-up existing shareholders are sometimes offered an opportunity to buy additional shares at a price below the market. Accordingly these rights are valuable. They are transferable, and it seems only reasonable that if there is a tax on the transfer of ownership of shares, the tax should likewise apply to transfers of rights to receive shares. This is what is proposed under resolution 1. Revenue from stock transfer tax for the latest fiscal year was about $1,000,000.

The government is doing something which more or less takes away from what the shareholders had to begin with. The government says, "We will put a little extra tax on this." I see no reason why you should want to tax these rights. It is not a heavy tax, but it adds up to a substantial amount over
Special War Revenue

a period. Will the minister agree that giving rights cannot possibly give a shareholder more than he had before? It merely prejudices him if he does not take up his rights.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I want to answer my hon. friend by saying that I am not trying to argue that his statement is a completely accurate statement of law. The granting of rights to a shareholder does not give him any greater interest in the company than he had before. But if he does not take up his rights but sells them, in effect he is selling a portion of his proportionate part of that company's business.
Mr.-JACKMAN: I will concede the fairness of a tax on the selling of the rights, but not on the exercise of the rights.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is no tax on the exercise of the rights; it is just a tax on the transfer or sale.
All right; that is fair.

These are the resolutions having to do with the Special War Revenue Act. Will the minister make a statement on the tax on soft drinks? There has been a good deal of concern about this tax; representations have been received from many young people, from church leaders, from leaders in the Boy Scout movement and other community leaders who have to do with our young people. They are all much concerned about this tax and I believe something should be done to reduce it. I should like to read a letter which I received from Reverend Joseph I. Monaghan, director of the Catholic youth organization, Immaculate Conception parish, Vancouver. It is as follows:
For almost twenty years I have had the high privilege of close association with and direct control of young people; and I believe my experience-in the classrooms of four provinces, as director of athletics at two colleges, and as moderator of young people's organizations- qualifies me to speak with authority on the attitude and tastes of youth.
Virtue has no more deadly enemy than strong drink. And plain, factual report should convince any honest citizen of our country that the "drink evil" is on the increase among our young people. Youth does not need any artificial stimulant for its social life and every effort should be made to have alcoholic drinks written off its beverage list. But we cannot ask our boys and girls to silence the natural clamour they all feel for the kind of beverage proper to their age. Whenever young people get together they drink. That is as common to them as eating potatoes. It is therefore the duty of every right-minded Canadian man and woman, and particularly of the Canadian government, to see that our boys and girls confine their drinking to beverages that give pleasure or quench thirst, without becoming habit forming as alcoholic stimulants do. Any step taken by the Canadian government to make soft drinks more easily available to young Canadians is a step in the right direction.

The special war excise tax levied on temperate beverages found our youth uncomplaining, and they gladly bore the expense and inconvenience of seven cents a bottle "pop." The war over, Canadian youth rightly believes this tax should be removed. In peace time it irritates them. They feel they should be granted again the right to buy their favourite beverage at the convenient pre-war price. Surely the government can meet the financial exigencies of the post-war period in some other way than by continuing a tax that young Canadians now strongly object to and which, if not removed immediately, will soon cause a loss of bountiful ood will that by no means can be compensated y the moneys acquired from a now unfair tax.
We leaders of youth in Canada have reason to believe that our government fully realizes and sincerely appreciates the contribution we are steadily making to our country by moulding the character of Canada's youthful citizens. That being so, may I respectfully beg you to assist us in our work by removing the cause of persistent annoyance felt by those under our charge.
I confidently assure you that compliance with this request will pay magnificent dividends.
Yours very truly,
(Rev.) Joseph I. Monaghan, S.J., Director, C.Y.O., Immaculate Conception Parish.
I do not pretend to be an expert on youth, although I have boys of my own, but I think Father Monaghan has placed his finger on the real significance of the effect of this tax. I suggest to the government that they would be wise to change it. I am not going to add to the submissions made in this letter, because they cover the case.

Like my hon. friend, I have received many letters of the kind, but I have taken exception to those letters. I have written back to priests and ministers and clubs pointing out that I was writing to the Minister of National Health and Welfare asking him to examine this whole soft drink question. To my mind it constitutes nothing more or less than a drug forming habit which is having its effect upon the lives of our people. I have had some experience in athletics, and I think any one who has had similar experience will agree that you would not ask an athlete to take soft drinks. There is nothing better than cold water when he is thirsty. I appeal to the minister of health to investigate this whole soft drink matter. I have not had an answer from any priest, minister or layman to my request that he make a statement in reply to my letter.
Does the hon. member consider that the drinking of cold water has made him the excellent bagpipe player that he is?

It has added a great deal to the strength of the playing.

Special War Revenue

'I did not rise to discuss the merits of various beverages from the athletic point of view, because I am no athlete. Like other hon. members I have received the usual, or in this case the almost unusual, number of letters advocating the removal of this tax. I have answered in every case that as far as I am aware there is no financial argument to be advanced in favour of removing tax at this particular time. I have confessed to those who wrote to me, and I declare now in this house that I am impressed by the argument that there is a moral side to the question which in my opinion transcends the importance of the tax value at the present time. I can have no idea what the situation would be in- the way of increased distribution of these beverages without knowing the facts as to the future distribution of glucose and sugar, which are the primary ingredients used by the manufacturers. I am not impresged by the suggestion made in some letters of possible political repercussions on the younger generation to be created by the removal of this tax.
I am sorry if my good friend the hon. member for New Westminster thinks me a sentimentalist. Perhaps I have not become as hardened as he professes to be to sentimental appeals, having received them over a smaller number of years than he has, but I am impressed by the appeals. I have had some experience and have knowledge of the nature of the social gatherings of young people. While we may not be able to establish as a temperance argument that seven cents for a soft drink is too close to the ten cents -for a beer, still there is a social question involved in the taxation. I have seen the benefits of youths' organizations. A considerable part of their social activities is associated with the availability of these soft drinks, and I would urge, together with others who have succumbed to these appeals, that the minister, even at this time, be less statistical and less concerned with the economic side of this matter, and review it again seriously, bearing in mind its social implications.

When I tried to get the floor a moment ago I had hopes that I could take a middle course between the views of the hon. member for Vancouver South and those of the hon. member for New Westminster. I believe there is a good deal of truth in what both of them have said. Like other hon. members I have received quite a number of communications regarding this tax. While agreeing with what the -hon. member for New Westminster said, that some check-up should be made as to the ingredients in some of these soft drinks, I feel that it is not the duty of
the Minister of Finance to deal with that; no doubt it comes under another department.
I said so.
I would say to the Acting Minister of Finance that I do not hesitate to tell those who write to me that in my opinion the two per cent tax is excessive.
Forty per cent.

It is altogether out of reason. During the time these letters have been arriving in the offices of members of parliament, the number in my mail dealing with this matter has run from twelve to fifteen or more per day. Many dozens of communications have been received by me from people in my constituency who are concerned about this tax. What I told my people back heme when I had an opportunity to speak to them on a number of occasions was this, that while I agreed that the tax was excessive, and that as the budget had not been brought down at that time we would have to wait and see what the Minister of Finance would do, I was disappointed in the attitude of our people when I got dozens of letters with regard to this tax on "pop" and did not get one single letter protesting the removal of the two cent subsidy on milk. It gives you some insight into the line of reasoning and thought in the minds of some people. When the two cent subsidy on milk was removed nobody was concerned, so far as my mail would indicate.
Come down to Toronto.
But when it came to "pop"-
"Pop goes the weasel."

It wentl With the hon. member for Vancouver South and others who have brought it to his attention, I would urge upon the minister that something be done to remove or reduce this excessive taxation, and at the same time that he advise his colleague in whatever department is concerned that in the opinion of many of us there should be some check-up of the ingredients in these soft drinks.

I should like to say a word in support of what the hon. member for Vancouver South has just said. I am not in agreement with the hon. member for New Westminster when he says this whole matter needs investigation. As a matter of fact, medical authorities in the United States have investigated these drinks again and again, and I have yet to see a report which is derogatory.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Oh, yes; we had one, when I was minister of health.
Special War Revenue

I have yet to see one. It seems to me ithat this is a matter of comparative values. Young people are drinking these soft drinks, and they are being sold at booths at every picnic throughout the country.
And right here in the house.

And right here in the house. People will drink these beverages. At the present time the tax on a bottle of pop amounts to 40 per cent. In the cafeteria we pay seven cents a bottle. So far as I am concerned I do not care if the use of these beverages is abolished entirely-I mean as far as the soft drinks are concerned.
Hear, hear!

But in these days, Mr. Chairman, when there is a considerable effort on the part of organizations throughout the country to combat juvenile delinquency occasioned by the consumption of hard liquor, I think we should at least pave the way to providing them with beverages which are not as harmful.
That may be the start of it.

To meet the minister half way, I say "as harmful". I admit that the consumption of soft drinks has increased, but so has our population increased1, and it is natural that with the increase of population the demand will increase. Also there is more money for people to buy drinks which otherwise might be considered as luxuries. Young people are consuming too much hard liquor; that is freely admitted; and if we can get them off the desire to use hard liquor by drinking a beverage which is not quite as harmful-if you like to put it that way, and I will grant the argument of the Minister of Veterans Affairs that probably it is harmful where it is not bottled under proper health regulations.
He does not know anything about it.

But that is not the argument. Every effort should be made to provide young people with these beverages at as low a cost as possible.
I am not concerned entirely with that, Mr. Chairman. It seems to me that there is another tax which we should have removed, and that is the tax on chocolate bars.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend a moment? I agreed a little earlier when a question was asked that it might be appropriate to have some discussion of the soft drink tax, because I know it is one concerning which hon. members have received a great many letters. There has been a very carefully organized campaign.
Don't put it on that basis.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not suggest that the letters are not sincere, but I know something of the background of the thing. However, we have had a very fair discussion, and I must insist that we do not go beyond this soft drink tax. I have a few observations to make on it, which will be brief, when the various members who wish to express their views have done so. But I do ask you, Mr. Chairman, to restrict the discussion. We are on a section dealing rvit'h the stock transfer tax, and we are talking about the soft drinks tax.
Do not put a tax on the beverage of the hon. member for New Westminster-cold water.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understood that there would be a limited discussion of the soft drinks tax. There has been quite a considerable discussion. Is it now the wish of the committee to hear the minister?

As one of the younger members of the 'house I wish to lodge a protest against all this talk about juvenile delinquency and the drinking of hard liquor. Listening to the discussion to-day one would think it was only the young people who do the drinking in this country. I believe that the greater proportion of drinking is done after the age of twenty-one. I have no objection to removal of the tax-it might be an advantage- but I would ask the minister, who has probably had some representations from the various bottling companies, whether he has had any assurance that if the two-cent tax is taken off the drinks will be sold at five cents as before. In the correspondence that I have had I have not been able so far to get that assurance, and it is an important question. If it is only a matter of removing the tax and keeping the price where it is, or reducing it one cent, there is not a strong case, but if it means a nickel drink, that is a recommendation for it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
On the last point, the Coca Cola people would give such an assurance, but there are a great many other bottlers and I do not know whether it is possible or feasible to get an assurance from them. Even if the tax were removed this year, however, it would not result in an added supply of soft drinks, because that is something that is controlled by the amount of sugar, which is in short supply, and every soft drink manufactured on the sugar quota is snapped up as fast as it gets into the hands of the vendors. There will be no added supplies available for soft drinks. The second point is this. Representations were made by the bottling companies-strong representations, I may say-and

Special War Revenue
it was felt that the tax should not be removed this year. Consequently there is no resolution providing for it.

There is one matter to which I should like to call the attention of the minister, but first I may say that I have not received a * great many communications with respect to the tax on soft drinks. In the city of Red Deer we have an establishment owned by an individual and engaged in the manufacture of soft drinks. I have visited his establishment within recent months. I have looked into his books. I find he has an investment of approximately $20,000. At the outbreak of the war he employed nine persons, and during the early years of the war a number of his employees enlisted. To-day, primarily because of the sugar quota, three persons working part time are able to manufacture all that the sugar quota will permit. But the argument is this. I can do that. It is a lengthy list, but I have a book here containing complete explanations of all items. Take tariff item No. 4, which relates to horses. This happens to be a new item. This item formerly provided for "horses, over one year old, valued at $100 or less per head" and carried rates of $10 per head under the British preferential tariff, $12.50 per head under the intermediate tariff, and $25 per head under the general tariff. The new item eliminates the words "over one year old, valued at $100 or less per head" and substitutes therefor the abbreviation "n.o.p."

Item 1 provides for duty free entry from all countries of pure bred horses for the improvement of stock. Item 4 covered horses over one year old valued at $100 or less per head and all other horses were included under item 5(c), the item covering living animals, n.o.p., duty free under the British preferential tariff, with a rate of 20 per cent under the intermediate tariff and 25 per cent under the general tariff. Under the present amendment all horses, except pure bred horses for the improvement of stock, are dutiable at rates of $10-$1250-$25 each.
This amendment facilitates the administration of the revised warehousing regulations issued by the Department of National Revenue on April 1, 1946. Under the former regulations it had been the practice of the Department of National Revenue to grant a racing bond for a period of ninety days to United States horses racing in Canada. This bond could be renewed when the horse moved from one track to another. At the end of the racing season the horses could be transferred to a feed and pasture bond which was good for twelve months. When the next racing season came along they could be transferred back to a racing bond, and so on indefinitely. The new regulations which went into effect on April 1, 1946, reduce the privileges enjoyed by race horse owners. If a horse leaves Canada to take part in a race in the United States it has to remain out of this country for three months before it may be reentered and bonded. It is permissible under the new regulations to transfer a horse racing in Canada from a racing bond to a feed and pasture bond, but it is not permissible to transfer from a feed and pasture bond to a racing bond without an intervening period of three months. A horse may remain under a feed and pasture bond for a period of not longer than nine months. When a horse is on a racing bond it must be transferred to a feed and pasture bond or returned to the United States where it must remain for a period of three months before reentering Canada.
Many of the horses which were in Canada on April 1, 1946, were United States horses owned by Canadians and were on a racing bond or a feed and pasture bond. When the bond expired these horses had to leave Canada or the owners had to clear them through customs by paying a duty of twenty per cent ad valorem, as in practically all cases they were over one year old and valued at over $100 each. Under the new item they may become Canadian horses by the payment of a duty of $1250 each. It is probable that most

Mr. ST. LAURENT: The legislature of Ontario adopted a bill providing for an increase of two in the number of judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario on the trial division, the amendment to come into force on proclamation. It has been represented to us, and we have found that the representations were justified by an examination of the facts, that in order to take care of the increasing volume of business in the trial division of the Ontario court it was necessary to increase the number of judges, because undue delays were occurring in the trial of cases in the high court. On the other hand, we represented to the authorities of Ontario that there might be some possibility of reducing below sixty-two the number of county court and district court judges in that province, and the attorney-general with his officials agreed to go carefully into an examination of that situation in an endeavour to bring down from sixty-two to fifty-two gradually, as vacancies would occur, the number of district and county court judges. I can assure the committee that the cooperation between the Department of Justice and the department of the attorney general in that regard has been harmonious, and that on both sides there has been an expressed and sincere desire to arrange the matter of the number of judges there so as to be of the greatest convenience to the public without increasing the expenditure to the country. It is felt that the work which has now to be handled by the county or district court judges could be handled by fewer judges if there were a better distribu-
tion of their time and services. Of course it will not be possible to remove judges for the purpose of decreasing the number; but, as vacancies occur, it is the hope that the number of judges of that court may ultimately be brought down from sixty-two to about fifty-two, and I undertook, in my negotiations with the attorney general of Ontario, to ask one of my colleagues to move an amendment to this section 7 which would allow, when the Ontario government has proclaimed its act, the appointment of two additional judges for the trial side of the supreme court of that province. Accordingly I would ask my colleague to move that paragraph (d) of clause 7 be amended by striking out the word "twelve" and substituting therefor, the word "fourteen".

I have raised the point before and I will not labour it on this occasion. I realize that the answer might very well be that they receive no salary in addition to their indemnity as judges. But amounts are paid of $15, $20 and even $25 a day while judges are serving on commissions. I agree absolutely with my right hon. friend, and I mention it again only because I feel that our purpose must be to secure the best men for the bench. While there are those who say that the best men can be obtained at present rates of indemnity, I join with the Minister of Justice in saying that I know men, leaders of the bar, who, within the last year or so in western Canada, never noted for great fees made by its counsel, have refused an offer to go to the bench, and in more than one instance have refused an offer to come to the Supreme Court of Canada.
I realize that we must secure the best men, and when the minister asks for an increase in Ontario to fourteen members on the bench, I would suggest that even then the members of the high court of justice in this province will be overworked. In large measure they are overworked to-day as a result of the tremendous volume of divorce litigation that is before the courts. Only the other day someone told me that in the city of Toronto alone there are 1,200 cases awaiting trial, and the same condition prevails everywhere across the dominion. I have no hesitation whatever in repeating what I said in this house two or three years ago, that some measure along this line ought to be introduced. I am sure I speak for the bar of this dominion when I say that the Minister of Justice has earned not only their gratitude but the gratitude of the people of Canada as a whole for introducing this measure. It may be subject to some criticism because other types of pension are not being raised at this time. I hear that argument advanced. For instance, there is the question of old age pensions. I should like to see old age pensions increased. But this measure is distinct and apart from that question.
This measure is one that strikes at the future of Canada, for, without a bench that is free from the suggestion of any possibility of taint, the administration of justice in this country cannot maintain in the minds of the people the high plane it now occupies. For years objections have 'been made by the bar association, and I say that one of the striking commendations of this bill is the fact that, without 63260-268
exception to my knowledge, the press of the dominion, realizing that there cannot be a free press unless the courts are untrammelled and are of the highest merit, have given unqualified support to this legislation.

The other day I asked the Minister of Justice a question with regard to the appeal court. I did not have all the information with reference to the matter. I have an item here which, with the Chairman's permission, I should like to read. It is from the Charlottetown Guardian of July 27, and reads as follows:
Under the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867, certain duties and obligations are imposed upon the province; others upon the dominion. It is the duty of the province, for instance, to declare what courts shall be constituted. This is done in the form of a provincial statute. It then becomes the duty of the dominion government to make appointments to the judiciary so constituted.
Such a statute was passed by the Prince Edward Island legislature in 1922. Chapter 6 of the statutes of that year enacted that "the bench of the said supreme court shall be composed of a chief justice and three other judges". That act was enacted in May, 1922, and was well within the legislative authority of the provincial legislature, under section 92 (14) of the British North America Act, 1867. Section 92 (14) declares that "in each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the class of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say: (14) The administration of justice in the province, including the constitution, maintenance and organization of provincial courts."
The question I asked the Minister of Justice the other day was how could they constitute a real court of appeal there.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: When I joined the Canadian government I had the advantage of having as one of my colleagues, a brilliant lawyer representing one of the constituencies pf Prince Edward Island and one who was much better informed of the situation in that province and of the needs in respect to the administration of justice there than I could be. We made serious efforts over a long period to find some system which would be acceptable to Prince Edward Island in respect of its judiciaiy appointed by the federal government. It was not found possible to do that unless we added an additional high court judge to the judiciary of that province. It was not felt that, it would be proper to do that in view of the fact that there were already three high court judges and three county court

judges there, and that the population was of numbers that are sufficiently provided for elsewhere by at most two judges. As I said to the hon. gentleman the other day, not knowing Prince Edward Island, but knowing the situation which prevails elsewhere, it seems to me that it would1 be in the interest of the people of that province if they had, rather than three high court judges and three county court judges, four high court judges and two county court judges. I am still hopeful that something along these lines can be worked out, because I appreciate that it would be more satisfactory if a three-man court could sit in appeal from the judgment of a court presided over by one high court judge. On the other hand, I would hesitate to recommend that there be an additional judge appointed for the judicial business to be transacted in that province. I assure the hon. gentleman that the question was considered sympathetically, and that my colleague of those diays, Hon. Mr. Ralston, did give it serious consideration and did try to devise some system which would not unduly increase the expenditure and which would be satisfactory to the people of my hon. friend's province. I still hope that that will be arrived at. It may be that this increase in salary will be helpful in that regard. I would not hesitate to recommend that there be four judges paid the increased salaries, provided that there were only two paid at the rate which prevails for county court judges.

I want to thank the minister for that good explanation. While I am not a lawyer, I still think one judge of the county court should be able to sit with the two supreme court judges in the court of appeal, two of them having an increase in salary.

Certainly it would require more

Judges Act
travelling on the part of district and county judges. Is the minister taking that into consideration?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes. Of course we take no initiative in determining the number of judges. We merely discuss the matter with the provincial authorities, because we feel they know better than we do the requirements of their respective localities. I wish to pay tribute to the good will and earnest endeavours I have met with everywhere in discussing a proper set-up for the administration of justice.

speechtext:

On section 19-Salaries of judges of circuit court of district of Montreal.

Apparently there is to be no increase in the amount allowed these two judges in the city of Montreal. My information is that the reason given is that the jurisdiction of the circuit court has been transferred to the superior court.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: To a magistrate's court set up and manned by the province.

I felt I should come before the house and say that this was not something being done for persons, that it was something done because I felt it was necessary or advisable in the interests of the public. I could not say that with respect to these two honourable gentlemen, most of whose work has been taken away from them and attributed to magistrates. They still have some cases within their jurisdiction, but there is very little for them to do and at the present time they cannot retire. When they reach the stage where they can retire they will get an annuity equal to the full salary attributed to their office at the time they were appointed.

How long have they been on the bench?

I felt, of course, that I could not ask parliament to take any right away from them, but that I would not be justified in asking parliament to give them, really as a retirement allowance, more than the salaries attributed to their offices at the time they were appointed, be-63260-268J
cause they have practically retired from the exercise of actual judicial functions, though they still conserve the judicial offices.

Has the minister given consideration to transferring these men to some position where, instead of waiting for the effluxion of time to bring them a pension, they would be able to give service for what they are receiving?

On section 20-Travelling allowances.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would ask my colleague to be good enough to move an amendment to this section. In drafting section 20 for the bill we did not give sufficient attention to the fact that certain county court judges are appointed for more than one county. The intention was not to deprive them of their allowance when they had to travel out of the county in which they reside. The intention of the clause was that they would1 not get travelling allowances for performing their judicial duties at the chief place of the county in which they reside, but it was not intended to deprive them of their right to travelling allowance when they had to go to another county where they had to perform judicial functions. I would, therefore, ask that subsection 4 of section 20 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
(4) No judge of a county court is entitled to be paid travelling allowance for attending in court or chambers at the county town of the county within which he resides or at the judicial centre or district town of the judicial district for which he is appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I move accordingly.

What is the meaning of that?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The meaning is that there must be one town at which the judge has to perform his judicial duties without being entitled to travelling allowances to go to that town. If he has more than one town where he has judicial duties to perform he shall be entitled' to travelling allowances for the other towns within which his commission normally requires him to operate. As the section was drawn previously it might have meant that he would not get a travelling allowance for attending at any of the court towns where under his commission he was required to perform his judicial duties. We wish to make it clear that it is only with
Judges Act

respect to the court town of the county in which he resides that he is not entitled to charge travelling expenses.

Will there have to be an amendment to subsection 5, or does this cover it?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not think any amendment is required there. He is not allowed travelling allowance for travel that is not necessary. If it is travel that is necessary, of course he makes the charge and receives the travelling allowance.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

May I ask the minister just how transportation expenses are calculated? I notice that later in the section there is an allowance for each day while away from home, we have just been discussing that. Does this transportation expense just cover his railway fare, or so much per mile for car operation if he uses an automobile? Does it include anything more?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It does not include anything beyond transportation and the specified allowance fixed by the statute.

I have not followed this very cliosely, but might I ask whether, when a county court judge who has more than one county under his jurisdiction goes to anothei county, he is allowed travelling expenses.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: He is allowed travelling expenses.

But as I read subsection 5 it does not say so. It says:
No judge of a county court is entitled to be paid travelling allowance for attending in court or chambers at a place not within the county-
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That is to take care of cases, which are quite frequent, where a judge goes into a county or district not normally within his jurisdiction to assist a brother judge or to replace a brother judge. In those cases there must be a certificate of the attorney general that the holding of court at that place was approved. But subsection 4 as now amended provides that the judge does not receive travelling allowances for attending at the county town of the county in which he resides. When he is appointed for more than one county, he receives travelling allowances for going elsewhere than to the court town of the county in which he resides.

Where does it say that?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: In the subsection as amended.

Do we presume that he is to be paid if he goes to another town?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes.

Is that only a presumption, or is it so stated?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That is stated in section 20 (1), in these words:
Subject as in this section provided, a judge of a superior or county court or a district judge in admiralty of the exchequer court who attends as such judge in court or chambers at any place other than that at which or in the immediate vicinity of which he is by law obliged to reside is entitled to be paid as a travelling allowance-
And so on.

It seems to me that this expense account of $10 a day is excessive. Officers of the armed services had to go into cities and towns, and all they were allowed was $6 a day. It seems to me that is enough?
I can see no reason for differentiation between a city and a town, because members of the armed services moved in and out of cities and towns, and they were allowed only S6.
I believe that is sufficient.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have seen accounts which indicate that it costs judges in Ottawa, Toronto, Quebec and Montreal more than the allowance provides. Representations were made that it should be increased. I said that I was not going to ask parliament to do more than to increase the salaries. It happens that they pay a little more than is allowed, but I did not want to ask parliament to make an increase in that allowance. However, I did see hotel bills, and I know that judges who travel almost every month from Montreal to Quebec and who stay at the Chateau Frontenac, and judges from Quebec who stay at the Windsor hotel in Montreal have expenses in excess of $10 a day.

speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Sections 21 to 24 inclusive agreed to.
On section 25-Compulsory retirement of judges of county court and circuit court of district of Montreal.

I note that under section 22, which deals with annuity on resignation, such annuity is not to be less than two-thirds of the salary. Under that provision, what would be the largest annuity, on retirement?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The largest annuity on retirement under this bill will be that to which the chief justice of the supreme court

Judges Act
will be entitled. No change is being made there. His retirement allowance will be equal to the salary of the office at the time he was appointed. That is because he was appointed prior to there being a retiring age fixed. It was felt that having a life tenure of office, and parliament having made the disposition that he could retire at the age of seventy-five, he should not be deprived of the emoluments of office. But in that respect no increase is being made. It was felt that that was a contractual right that it would not be proper to change, but that we were not required to extend it when an increase was being made in annual salaries.
County or district court judges are also required to retire at the age of seventy-five. Under the former act they retired with an annuity equal to full salary. That number of dollars is not being increased. We say we will increase their salaries, but we do not recognize any obligation to increase the retiring allowance to which they were entitled under the present act.
Then the hon. member asked what would be the largest retiring allowance in respect of the other judges. The next largest would be for the puisne judges of the supreme court, who would receive two-thirds of $16,000. All the other retiring allowances are two-thirds of the stated salary.

Has a fund been set up to provide these annuities, and have the judges contributed to such fund, as do civil servants?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No, there never has been any fund provided for retiring allowances. It has never been on a contributory basis. Our system was borrowed from the British system, and I think it antedates the establishment of superannuation funds for civil servants. It is something we inherited when we inherited the system, and it has been conserved since.
I hope it is in order to make the remark I am going to make. I was thinking that the non-pensionable war widows are going to love this.

When we suggest that annuities should be paid in other cases, the argument in advanced to us that it detracts from a person's self-respect to draw from an annuity to which he has not contributed. But apparently on this level it does not affect them in any way.

Recently Mr. Justice Plaxton retired because of illness. Would he come within the provisions of section 22? What would his retirement allowance be?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: His retirement allowance was $4,000, because he had exercised the option provided in the 1944 statute. As the hon. member has noted, there is no attempt here to increase the retiring allowance of those who retired hitherto.
I appreciate that.

Is there any retroactive
measure with regard to pensions?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No.

Either for the wife or the judge?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. There is nothing being done with respect to judges who have retired hitherto, because it was felt that their annuities were not payable to them under the terms of the statute, but because they had received letters patent granting them stated annuities. The Judges Act, so far as they were concerned, had been exhausted. They had been given what the Judges Act empowered the government to give them, namely letters patent providing a stated annuity. But it was not felt that the process of amending the Judges Act could or should have any effect upon what had been done in the past.

If a judge retires before the retiring age would that affect his pension?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I may have to qualify my answer. There is a retiring age only for federal court judges and district and county court judges. The federal court judge is required to retire at seventy-five years. There is no provision for these judges retiring before that time unless they become incapacitated. If they become incapacitated they can be retired and receive a pension equal to two-thirds of the salary attached to their office. A county court judge can retire with pension- this has not been changed-after thirty years of service, payable at the same rate as would be paid if he retired at the age of seventy-five years; that is, a pension of $5,000. After twenty-five years service he can retire, if the lieutenant governor states in the acceptance of the resignation that it is in the public interest that he should' retire, with a pension of two-thirds the salary.

speechtext:

Section 26 agreed to.
On section 27-Annuity provision in respect to judge taking public office.

Perhaps the minister could answer the question which I asked a week or so ago with respect to Mr. Justice Davis, a judge of the court of appeals of Saskatchewan, who since his first appoint-
Judges Act

ment has served, first, on the board administering the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act; second, as deputy minister of national war services and, latterly, as minister to Australia. There have been a number of references in the press to the fact that he is to leave the bench to enter the diplomatic service, either in Washington or in London. I would appreciate if the minister would outline exactly what his position would be with regard to pension and the extent to which the period that he had been a judge although not actively serving as a judge would count in the payment of an annuity.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: With respect to Mr. Justice Davis this section will provide, as it has already been provided with respect to the chief commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, that when he retires from the public service he will be in the same position as if he were retiring from the bench. If he were dismissed from the public service before serving fifteen years from the time of his first appointment to the bench, under the terms of the act he would not be entitled to receive a pension.

To be concrete in the matter, Mr. Justice Davis has been eight years as a member of the bench although not actually serving on the bench. If he retires in order to enter the diplomatic service, what will be his pension for the time he was actually appointed to the bench?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No pension while in the public service and no pension if dismissed from the public service before fifteen years from the time of bis original appointment to the bench. But if he retires from the public service at a time when the governor in council might certify that his retirement from the bench was in the public interest he will then receive a pension equal to two-thirds of the salary attached to the office of judge.

I am trying to follow that. I presume that if he is appointed to a diplomatic post he will not continue as a member of the bench in Saskatchewan; I presume also that the governor in council will grant him permission to retire as judge. As my right hon. friend knows, if there is one thing more necessary than another it is that a judge serve on the bench to which he has been appointed. In Saskatchewan the court of appeal is made up of five members who necessarily have to deal with abstruse points of law, There should be an odd member on the bench in order to guard against dismissals of appeal because of an equal distribution of opinion on the bench. If Mr. Justice Davis receives a
rMr. Diefenbaker.]
diplomatic appointment, will he then be permitted to retire and what will be his pension? I am asking this question of the right hon. gentleman both in his capacity as Minister of Justice and as Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: He would receive no pension upon being appointed to the service of external affairs and he would receive no pension while in office with external affairs. Upon retirement from external affairs he would be entitled to be granted the same pension as if at the moment he were retiring from the bench.

In other words, he gets a judge's pension?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: He would get his judge's pension when retiring from the public service if he served another seven years.

I think this is an unusual proceeding. It means that we are going to place our judges on the bench where, once appointed, one believes they will serve so long as they have the capacity. We are going to place our judges in the position where they will accept appointments to the bench as a temporary expedient and then, after a few - years on the bench, take some other appointment, possibly some semi-political appointment. Then, having served in that capacity for a period of years and finally terminating their services they are able to count not only the period they served as judges but also the period in the public service.
I should like to know the extent to which there has been a demand for this change in the law. I am fearful of the prospect that the separation of judiciary and executive will not be as complete as it should be should parliament give approval to a plan such as this. I would not object if a judge retired from the bench with the consent of the government and then received a pension at the conclusion of his public service for the period that he had actually served on the bench. That would be going a long way, but this is going a long way farther. I should like to know whether it is to cover an ad hoc case, or is it anticipated by the minister that there will be a number of cases such as this where judges retire from the bench after a few years to take up other types of public service where no pension is payable and then, having taken up that other type of public service, be rewarded with a pension as though they had already served on the bench?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed consideration in committee of bill No. 250, respecting judges of dominion and provincial courts-Mr. St. Laurent-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONSOLIDATION AND AMENDMENTS OP ACT- SALARIES, ETC.
speechtext: The committee is considering section 27.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION AND AMENDMENTS OP ACT- SALARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I return once more to this section to make a few observations. The reason the judiciary enjoys the high reputation it does lies in the fact that when a person is appointed to the bench it is generally conceived that in that situation he gives no further consideration to any question of participation in public affairs. If there is one thing more than another that should be kept in mind it is that, once a judge is appointed to the bench, unless he chooses to retire, to divest himself of the position and of any emoluments pertaining thereto, there should be no suggestion that he might be open to consider the acceptance of a position paying more than does the judiciary. And after he has had an opportunity of serving in a more highly paid position for a period of years, to suggest that at the conclusion of his term he should receive a pension such as a judge receives, is a dangerous principle.
I realize a somewhat similar principle was partly in effect previously to cover the position of chief commissioner or assistant chief commissioner of the board of railway commissioners, both those positions being pseudojudicial, or semi-judicial positions ordinarily to be filled by outstanding jurists or men learned in the law. But to extend this principle so that a judge, after serving a few years on the bench, may retire therefrom and then accept some position in the public service,

Judges Act
and at the end of his term in the public service reap the advantages that were his by reason of the sacrifice he made in his income in going on the bench, if he is a leading member of the bar, seems to me to be a dangerous principle to adopt.
I would ask the minister to inform the committee how many judges he has in mind who are about to retire, or is this an ad hoc proposition to meet one specific case? I should like to know what representations have been made to this end by the Canadian Bar association. I believe I speak with knowledge and certainty when I say that in Great Britain, where our entire judicial system was born and nurtured, there is no equivalent to this proposition.
I do not wish to raise smoke-screens, but I feel that when we place our judges in a posi-' tion of inviolability on the bench, when we guarantee them the increased salaries that they will now receive under this bill, when we guarantee them, after years of service, a substantial and reasonable retirement allowance and pension, there should not be admitted the principle of dangling before judges the opportunity of accepting positions in the public service paying more, accepting such positions for a period of years and then at the end of that term asking the country to give them a pension not only for the years they served on the bench but also for the period of years they served in the public service additionally.
The committee, I suggest, deserves a fuller and more complete explanation of the section. It is a novel departure, one that is easily passed and in which there may lie implications which at the moment we can only contemplate. If there is one thing more than another we must do, so far as the judiciary is concerned, it is to keep it above the suggestion of political considerations. If we place our judges in a position where, having once established the right to a pension on going on the bench, they may retire therefrom and accept positions in the public service, reaping the advantage of the pensions that are paid to those who enter the judiciary, then the door is open to situations which at the moment I do not care to suggest to the committee but which I believe everyone here can appreciate.
Has this section been submitted to the Canadian Bar association? Where is the demand for the change in the law which is proposed in this section, and what particular case or cases is it contemplated will come within the ambit of this provision at an early day?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: In Canadian history I know of only two cases which it was intended 63260-269
to have covered by this legislation and by its prototype which was adopted in 1931 under a former administration. At that time it was desired to have the services of a gentleman who, if I mistake not, was on the bench in tne province of Manitoba, become chief railway commissioner, because it was felt that he was the proper person to fill the office. It would appear that, having a life tenure on the bench, with the advantages that come from the pension provisions, he would not agree to the change without a provision such as this being made, and it was made by legislation in 1931.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION AND AMENDMENTS OP ACT- SALARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Is that not a semijudicial appointment?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have described it. The hon. member knows as I do what functions are performed by the board of railway commissioners. It was found at that time by the former administration that legislation of this kind, to enable the country to obtain the services of that gentleman in that capacity, was desirable. Now, more recently, it was found that another justice who had performed valuable services to the country during the war period had shown special qualifications for the diplomatic service. It was also found that that gentleman felt, as did the judge of the Manitoba court in 1931, felt that it was not proper to ask him to abandon the life tenure which was his by virtue of his appointment, and since it was desired to have his services in a diplomatic capacity it was felt that the provision which had been made in 1931 might, by a slight change in phraseology, be made to apply in this case. That is the only reason this section was drawn in the form in which it is presented to the committee. I know of no other prospective case.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION AND AMENDMENTS OP ACT- SALARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Who is the Manitoba judge?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Judge Fullerton. I know of no other case, and I know of very few posts in the public service which would come under the description of "more lucrative" used by the hon. gentleman when this bill will have become law. I do not know of many posts in the public service which will prove to be more attractive in the w'ay of remuneration and security of tenure than what we are providing for the judges. I think that is as it should be. I think these high judicial posts should be among the things to which lawyers would aspire as being the best that they can achieve. I would not anticipate that there could be very many cases where this clause would operate. From 1931 to 1946 it operated only once, and from now on I have in mind1 this special case where I think the result would appear to be com-

Judges Act

patible with public interest. I think the gentleman in question has shown remarkable ability in the discharge of diplomatic duties, and I think it might be of advantage to the state if these exceptional qualities which he has displayed remained available to the state in that capacity; but at this time that will require that he resign from the bench.
During the war it was possible to ask brother judges to do more than under normal conditions, but I think it would be intolerable to leave, during normal times which I hope we are getting to or will get to pretty soon, actual vacancies that could not be filled in the judicial set-up which is required for the proper administration of justice. I think one must be one thing or the other, and that it is necessary now to have a solution of this situation which, could be tolerated during the war period, but should not be allowed to continue indefinitely.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION AND AMENDMENTS OP ACT- SALARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am wondering whether there is any definite term during which a judge would have to be on the bench before this provision became operative. May a judge serve on the bench for a year and then be transferred to a public office, and when he leaves that public office become entitled to pension rights as if he remained on the bench for ten years or more, and in the event of his death his widow be entitled to her pension rights? It seems to me that this is an amazing provision, and if there is anything more amazing it is the arguments with which the Minister of Justice supported it.
A week ago when we last discussed this bill I was given to understand that there Was great difficulty in securing good men to take positions on the bench because the remuneration of the office was not adequate. I am glad to support the point made by the hon. member for Lake Centre in opposition to section 27 of this bill. As I see it, it is important, in order that we may have an efficient judiciary, that judges be well indemnified so that they may be free of financial worries, to the extent that we may reasonably do so. I believe that is the fundamental principle behind the intention of the government to increase the salaries of judges. Under the salaries in effect up to the present time, I believe that men who otherwise might accept judicial appointments have not done so because of the much greater remuneration they would receive in private practice. This section, however, deals with a man who has held high public office, with great responsibility. It has been argued that the same reasons which support increasing the salaries of judges to give them greater security and immunity from worry would also support the same action in regard to those holding public office; but why should we confuse the two? Why should we say that a man who has held high office in the public service, with great responsibility and, of course, reasonably good remuneration, should have to rely upon the fact that previously he had been a member of the judiciary in order to get what is given to him under this section? In other words,

Judges Act
take two men, one accepting public office not having been a judge, the other accepting public office after having been on the bench. There may be a vast difference in what these men are entitled to under this provision. If high remuneration must be offered to encourage men to accept high political office, it should be put upon that basis only, and not on the basis that a man was a member of the bench prior to accepting public office.
There is another reason for providing pensions for judges and persons holding high public office, and for their widows and families; that is the reason of necessity. Surely a man wdio leaves the judiciary to accept high public office should not be considered as in such . necessitous circumstances as to require this provision. Surely it would be a disgrace and an indictment against our country if we should go to a member of the judiciary and say, "You are the only man who can do this job; come with us," and then say that after he has served the country with his high qualities we shall treat him as though he needed a pension, or his widow and family needed it. When the minister said in reply to the hon. member for Lake Centre that he knew of no appointments more lucrative or more secure than judgeships he uttered a strong indictment against the very principle of the bill which I approve. I believe it is a fact that the men who have accepted judgeships have not been given the highly lucrative positions and the security it is necessary to offer in order to get the right men in the right places, administering their duties in the right way. If that is the fundamental principle behind this bill 'the answer of the minister was a great disappointment to me and, I am sure, to- other hon. members, because I do not think that is a point which should be taken. I do not believe it is a matter of necessity. I believe it is a matter of wanting to get the best men available both for the judiciary and for high public office. I would not say which were needed most; but I should say that in appointments which carry with them the trust of the government, reliance should be placed upon the compensation, the security, the immunities and so on that the office itself merits, without having to rely upon the previous occupation of one who is appointed.
Therefore I think it would be a mistake to pass section 27 as it stands and create discrimination among those holding high public office, as between those who once were judges and those who were not. They should be able to hold and 63260-269J

The reason for my being in substantial agreement with them and for my being opposed to section 27 is that I believe it violates one of the most fundamental principles of retirement allowances. In the case of a contributory system where a person is given leave of absence for a specified period of time from his regular duty in the profession or occupation which would give him his retirement allowance upon retirement, the period for which he is granted leave of absence is based on his term of service. If he goes back to his original profession or service he then would be granted the pension upon reaching the age of retirement, just as if he had not been granted leave of absence. With that principle I am thoroughly in agreement. But in this case there is no desire or intention to adhere to that principle. If the principle is sound for contributory systems, then it must be more than sound for non-contributory systems.
Rather than to press for section 27 I would suggest to the minister that he give consideration to adopting the principle of a specific period leave of absence. After the termination of that specific period, the judge could return to his judicial duties and serve out his time. Then, when he was ready to retire under the regular term of judges' retirement, give him his pension. That procedure would he in strict conformity with the best practices of retirement allowances. I find myself quite opposed to the suggestion as it is to-day.

No judge of a superior or county court shall he granted leave of absence from his judicial duties for a period in excess of thirty days except with the approval of the governor in council, and whenever such leave of absence is granted, the Minister of Justice shall forthwith notify the chief justice, if any, of the court and the attorney general of the province accordingly.
